# SpaceX Sits Pretty While Anthropic Keeps Cursor Close — And OpenAI Keeps Cutting

OpenAI just made it harder for competing AI coding tools to use its models. Anthropic responded by doubling down on Cursor. And somewhere in the middle, SpaceX is sitting in what one observer called an "enviable position."

This isn't about rockets. It's about who controls the tools your developers use every day.

## What Actually Happened

OpenAI recently cut off or restricted API access for several AI-powered coding assistants that compete with its own products. The move hit tools that had been built on top of OpenAI's models — and it sent a clear signal about how the company sees the competitive landscape.

Anthropic went the other direction. Instead of pulling back, the company is sticking with Cursor, the AI coding assistant that's been gaining traction with engineering teams. Anthropic's Claude models power a significant chunk of Cursor's capabilities, and that partnership isn't going anywhere.

SpaceX enters the picture because of its unique infrastructure position. The company runs its own compute, operates outside the typical cloud provider dependencies, and doesn't have to pick sides in the OpenAI-Anthropic turf war. That's the "enviable position" — when your AI tooling doesn't depend on a single vendor who might change the rules tomorrow.

## What This Means for Teams Using AI Coding Tools

If your team built workflows around an AI assistant that relies on OpenAI's API, you're now exposed to platform risk. Not theoretical risk — actual risk that your tooling could degrade or disappear based on a vendor's competitive strategy.

This is the classic build-on-a-platform problem. When the platform decides you're a competitor, you lose.

Cursor users get a different story for now. Anthropic seems committed to the partnership, which gives Cursor some stability. But "for now" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

## What This Is Not

This is not a signal that OpenAI's models are suddenly worse, or that Anthropic's are suddenly better. Model quality is a separate question from business strategy.

This is also not a reason to panic-migrate your entire toolchain overnight. But it is a reason to ask some uncomfortable questions:

- How dependent is your AI-assisted workflow on a single model provider?
- What happens if that provider decides your tool is competition?
- Do you have a fallback, or are you locked in without knowing it?

The teams in the best position right now — like SpaceX — are the ones who either built flexibility into their stack or have enough leverage that vendors won't cut them off.

Most teams don't have SpaceX's resources. But you can still reduce your exposure by choosing tools that support multiple model backends, or at least by understanding exactly where your dependencies are.

## [CHRIS TAKE]

## The Question Worth Asking

The AI coding tool market is consolidating fast. OpenAI wants to own the whole stack — models and the products built on them. Anthropic is playing a different game, at least for now, by supporting third-party tools like Cursor.

Neither approach is inherently better for your team. What matters is whether you're paying attention to the dependencies you're creating.

If your developers love their AI assistant and it works great today, that's fine. Just know who controls it. And have a plan for when the rules change.

Because they will.
